summary: Authoring craft for the brand voice guide as an artifact. The output is a document other writers will open, reference, and apply.

facts.text: Authoring craft for the brand voice guide as an artifact. The output is a document other writers will open, reference, and apply.
A brand voice guide answers four questions for every writer who opens it:
Who do we sound like? (Voice - the constant.)
How do we shift in different situations? (Tone - the variable.)
Which words do we use, and which do we never use? (Vocabulary.)
What does this look like in practice? (Examples - usually do/don't pairs.)
If a guide doesn't make these four questions answerable in under 10 minutes of reading, it will be ignored.
Voice - three to five attributes that describe the constant personality. State each as "We are X. We are not Y." (Bloomstein's BrandSort framing: include the not.)
Tone - a matrix showing how voice flexes by situation.
Vocabulary - preferred words, banned words, and grammar/style decisions specific to the brand.
Examples - at least 5 do/don't pairs spanning the highest-traffic surfaces.

facets.title: 2. Voice attributes — the "we are X, we are not Y" pattern

facts.text: The canonical format:

> Confident, not arrogant. We make declarative claims when we know we're right. We don't oversell, hedge with weasel words, or talk down to readers who know less than us. > > Warm, not saccharine. We sound like a competent colleague who likes their job. We don't use exclamation marks to perform enthusiasm or call readers "friend."
Three to five attributes is the sweet spot.
The Nielsen Norman Group axes: formal↔casual, serious↔funny, respectful↔irreverent, enthusiastic↔matter-of-fact.
Anti-pattern: Putting all markers in the middle. "Moderately formal, moderately serious, moderately enthusiastic" is no voice.

facets.title: 5. Do/don't pairs (the "this but not that" convention)

facts.text: > Do: "We paused your build. Resume it when ready." > Don't: "Oops! Looks like your build got paused. No worries - just click Resume whenever you'd like to keep going! 🚀"
The don't side teaches more than the do side. Pick don'ts from real drafts your team has actually shipped.

facets.title: 6. Vocabulary section: preferred, banned, and decisions

facts.text: Preferred - words that carry the voice. ("ship" not "release"; "you" not "the user".)
Banned - words that break the voice. ("leverage", "synergy", "seamless", "robust", "delightful", "passionate".)
Decisions - product-name capitalization, oxford comma, contractions allowed, em dash vs en dash.
Every voice guide should display:
Version (semver or date)
Last reviewed date
Owner (a person, not a team)
Next review date (no more than 12 months out)
No "we are not." Lists three positive attributes with no opposites.
Spectrum markers all centered. "Moderately formal" is no guidance.
Don't-side strawmen. Don't pairs that are obviously bad teach nothing.
No date, no owner. Writers won't trust an undated guide.
30+ page voice guide. Anything past 10 pages won't be read.
Banning words without preferring others. "Don't say leverage" without "say use" leaves writers stuck.
No tone matrix. Writers can match personality but not situation.
Mailchimp Content Style Guide - Voice and Tone
Atlassian Design - Voice and Tone
Bloomstein, M. Content Strategy at Work. Morgan Kaufmann, 2012.
Fenton, N. and Kiefer Lee, K. Nicely Said. New Riders, 2014.
Nielsen Norman Group - The Four Dimensions of Tone of Voice
A team produces content across multiple writers — marketing, support, product copy — and needs one reference so voice doesn't drift depending on who wrote the sentence.
